description: Stacks, tabs, drawers, modals, and deep links.

screens.body:
The most common mobile navigation is a stack: each new screen is pushed on top, and going back pops it off. It's like a stack of cards — you always see the top one, and 'back' reveals the one underneath.

Almost every drill-down flow (list → detail → edit) is a stack. If your user can go deeper, you need a stack.

options: Push a screen on top; back pops it off
check.question: In stack navigation, opening a detail screen means…

code.snippet:
const stack = ['Home'];
stack.push('Orders');      // go deeper
stack.push('Order #42');   // deeper still
stack.pop();               // back -> 'Orders'
console.log(stack[stack.length - 1]); // 'Orders'

screens.heading: The navigation stack
screens.keyPoint: Push to go deeper, pop to go back.

screens.body:
Tabs are for top-level sections the user switches between constantly: Home, Search, Cart, Profile. Three to five tabs is the sweet spot — more than that and labels get cryptic.

Each tab usually keeps its own stack. Switching tabs shouldn't lose your place: jumping from Search back to Home should return you to where you were in Home.
screens.heading: Tabs for top-level sections
screens.keyPoint: 3–5 tabs; each keeps its own place.

screens.body:
A drawer (the 'hamburger' menu) slides in from the side and can hold many destinations — great for apps with lots of sections. The downside is discoverability: out of sight, out of mind.

Use drawers for secondary destinations users visit occasionally: settings, help, about. Keep the daily-use stuff in tabs where it's always visible.

check.question: A drawer menu is best for…

screens.heading: Drawers and menus
screens.keyPoint: Drawers hide things — fine for secondary screens.

screens.body:
A modal slides up and demands attention: 'finish this first.' Log in, compose a message, confirm a payment — then it dismisses and you're back where you were.

Because modals interrupt, use them sparingly. A modal for every little thing trains users to dismiss without reading, which defeats the point.

options: A screen that interrupts: finish this first
A screen you can never close
check.question: A modal is…

screens.heading: Modals interrupt
screens.keyPoint: Modals demand focus — spend that sparingly.

screens.body:
Screens often need data: the detail screen needs to know which order to show. You pass small parameters — route params — like orderId: 42. The screen then loads the full data itself.

Keep params tiny: IDs and flags, not whole objects. Passing big objects between screens duplicates memory and goes stale.

check.question: Pass between screens as route params…

screens.heading: Passing data between screens

screens.body:
A deep link is a URL that opens a specific screen: myapp://orders/42, or a normal https link that the OS routes into your app. They're how push notifications, emails, and ads land users exactly where they should be.

Every important screen should have a deep-linkable address. Test them — a notification that opens the wrong screen is worse than no notification.

options: A URL that opens a specific app screen
A link to the app store
check.question: A deep link is…

screens.heading: Deep links
screens.keyPoint: Every important screen deserves a linkable address.

screens.body:
Android has a system back button (or gesture) that the user expects to work everywhere. iOS relies on the in-app back button. Your navigation has to honor both.

Decide what system-back does on each screen: pop the stack, close the modal, or — on the home screen — maybe ask 'press back again to exit.' Never let it silently dump the user somewhere weird.

options: Honor it: pop the stack or close the modal
check.question: When the user hits Android's system back button, you should…

screens.heading: The Android back button
screens.keyPoint: System back must do something sensible on every screen.
